 Video, Audio, Photos & Rush Transcript: Governor Hochul Delivers Welcome Remarks at Ceres Climate Week

 Video, Audio, Photos & Rush Transcript: Governor Hochul Delivers Welcome Remarks at Ceres Climate Week 

 Governor Hochul: “I'm still fighting back against Washington, but it's been harder to meet the goals that we set forth because of these unforced errors and unprecedented assault on our ambition. [...] But these new investments are real exciting for us. And so I just want to encourage all of you. We're doing 95 large-scale solar, wind, hydro and offshore wind projects right now, delivering 10.5 gigawatts of clean power, more than 4.6 million homes. I want clean, affordable power for families, but I'm not going to have an economy that's stuck in the past.”
 Hochul: “It would be smart money to invest for sure in a place like New York because I’ll break down any barrier that stands in our way of doing what I need to do to support my economy, to keep the lights on, to drive down costs for consumers and create thousands of good paying clean energy jobs. So we’re ambitious.”

 Governor Hochul today addressed business, finance and policy leaders at the Ceres Climate Week Event in New York City, touting New York’s record of ambition and execution, including her nation-leading efforts on offshore wind, solar energy, her plans for expanded nuclear energy, and her signature AI moratorium. The Governor outlined what New York has been doing to overcome federal headwinds due to reckless Republican policies that New York and other states face in their efforts to address climate change while trying to keep the lights on and costs down. She also urged investors to “step up” in New York’s efforts to increase clean energy supply.
 VIDEO: The event is available to stream on YouTube here and TV quality video is available here (h.264, mp4). 
 AUDIO: The Governor's remarks are available in audio form here. 
 PHOTOS: The Governor’s Flickr page will post photos of the event here. 
 A rush transcript of the Governor's remarks is available below: 
  I never felt so tall in front of a podium, holy smokes. Thank you, Mindy. Mindy Lubber has been an extraordinary global leader in this space, to talk about the intersection of investment, but also achieving ambitious goals, and I love that we have people who understand that dynamic and who talk about it and bring people together to find not just the ambition, but also the execution, which is what we're all about here in New York. I want to thank her. Also, Doreen Harris, who's representing me at probably 4,000 events this week. She is a national leader. If you want to know what's going to be happening in this country, because New York always leads, you talk to Doreen Harris. She will tell you where we're headed. She's the head of NYSERDA and has done an extraordinary job, and I thank her for everything she's done for our administration. Also we're joined by our Comptroller Mark Levine, who's been a longtime climate activist as well. Proud to have our association as well.
 So here we are. Welcome to New York. Anybody complain about the traffic? I want to tell you this, if we didn't enact the first ever in America congestion pricing, it'd be a lot worse, okay? Just want to put that out there. I'm a New Yorker, I have to brag. Knicks in five, everything. We've had a great year. But I'm really proud to host you and those who are joining us online.
 As I mentioned, ambition matters, but execution is everything. And I literally had a conversation — I was out on Long Island late last night — and someone says, “What keeps you up at night? What are your fears?" And I had to say, which is what keeps me up at night, is solving our energy crisis, right now. I have to figure out how to power this state that has come perilously close to having brownouts and blackouts as we've been battered with really unpredictable, unprecedented winter storms. We lost 17 people in those storms just a few months ago, last winter here in New York City. I'm from Buffalo, we had our worst blizzards — we had seven feet of snow recently. As someone who grew up with blizzards, this is next level blizzards.
 And as a governor who's been in office just since 2021 — a little bit unexpectedly, there's a history there — but my first week on the job, we had two hurricanes. We had more hurricanes in New York than we had in Florida that year. Of course, I'm brand new Governor, like, “Am I supposed to declare an emergency? What do I do with this?" It was an unprecedented time and also a challenge for my new administration to figure this out, but now, it's becoming the norm. I mean, they're predicting we might have a pretty bad storm this weekend.
 And so execution is everything. So I believe that it's not an either/or proposition — that we're going to fight for climate change or protect us from climate change and to have smart strategies, but we're also going to power our states. They have to help each other. They have to coexist, and I think for a long time it was an one or the other, and in New York, we're smarter than that. We know how to do both. We can walk and chew gum at the same time in New York. We do it all the time. So I'm proud to be able to be in a position — I'm going to be named one of the co-chairs of the US Climate Alliance next spring. I've held that role earlier. Looking forward to charting a path forward for the nation as well. And I get a chance to work with brilliant governors — I was just with many of them yesterday, and what a dream team we have of US governors who are really working with us to confront the two crises at the same time.
 And demand is rising for energy as well. [At] the same time we're trying to deal with what is happening with Mother Nature and decades of assault on Mother Nature — I say mankind's assault on Mother Nature, it wasn't womankind, it was mankind's assault. It was the men who were building the factories up where I grew up in Buffalo, on the shores of Lake Erie, where I grew up. And I thought the skies were supposed to be orange, because that's what I saw billowing out of the steel plant where my dad worked, my uncles worked. It was the bread and butter. It was our economy. Nobody questioned the fact that this huge factory, every night, would dump tons of this orange molten lava into one of the greatest freshwater lakes on the planet. And then we swam in it. So when I talk about environmental activism, it's in my DNA, so I know how bad it can be.
 And we've had policies for many years, starting with 1972 and the creation of the EPA, and believe it or not, it was Richard Nixon who brought us to a better place, so we're more thoughtful about our overt contamination of our resources. That's good. But how we also talk about what has been happening with greenhouse emissions globally, what effect that has had on our weather changes, and I don't — we have climate deniers, we have AI impact deniers, we have crazy people speaking [before] the UN yesterday, but I won't diverge too much. So that's what we're up against.
 We know what we have to do. In this room, we know what we have to do. But let me tell you some of the challenges, and I'm trying to create a clean energy future here in the State of New York and powers — I like offshore wind. We're proud of what we have. Doreen, aren't we the largest — what is it? Largest commercial grade scale — we got all these metrics — okay, we're the best in America, just take it from me. But we want to do more, and now this administration in Washington has shut down any more lease opportunities, projects that literally take 10 years to come to fruition.
 One: Empire Wind. Ten-year plan, $5 billion investment, foreign investment, local investment, thousands of good-paying jobs for our union workers. It's our dream. This is a really great project, and I'm so excited to go to all sorts of milestone announcements, we're getting it done. And all of a sudden, Donald Trump gets in office and decides, "I don't like offshore wind." And he shuts it down. I have to get on the phone. I have to go visit in Washington. It's like:
 "What's the problem with offshore wind, Mr. President?"
 "It kills the birds."
 "Didn't know you were so concerned about the birds."
 He killed it. Shut it down. We lost all this money, and literally the project was going to disappear, and we had to beg the company not to close up shop. They're losing $50 million a week, and we got them to hang on, and that's to power 500,000 homes in Brooklyn. That's what we're trying to do. Look at the headwinds we have. So we get stymied there.
 Onshore wind, solar. Now I'm going to tell you, because you can look up how old I am, I'm really old, and I was a young staffer working on Capitol Hill back in the '80s when President Reagan came in and wiped out all the energy initiatives that Jimmy Carter had started during the oil embargo and the energy crisis, when I still walk out of every room and turn off the lights because Jimmy Carter told us to, okay? And keep the temperature down and wear a sweater in the house. That is still in my head. We had solar tax credits, we had wind tax credit, we had all kinds of innovative strategies, electric vehicles, all sorts of incentives at a time for these new industries to really take off, and they were going to be incredible. And the Republicans take office in the White House, and Ronald Reagan shuts it all down. And I just knew at that moment as a young staffer that this could be decades in the making of trying to bring it all back.
 And so we've overcome those challenges as well. I'm still fighting back against Washington, but it's been harder to meet the goals that we set forth because of these unforced errors and unprecedented assault on our ambition. So we're committed to carrying on despite this, I believe in elections, every couple years have a chance to reset, okay? Break the fever, get back to normal. It'll get there. But these new investments are real exciting for us. And so I just want to encourage all of you. We're doing 95 large-scale solar, wind, hydro and offshore wind projects right now, delivering 10.5 gigawatts of clean power, more than 4.6 million homes. I want clean, affordable power for families, but I'm not going to have an economy that's stuck in the past.
 When I was Lieutenant Governor, I knew about this project, and nothing was happening for years — we could bring clean hydroelectric power from Quebec down to power New York City. It could've been done five years earlier. It was brought to the previous administration. During Climate Week, my first year in office, 2021, I announced, “I'm going to get that done,” and I went up to Quebec, met with the premier, met with everybody and said, "I want this done." What a great concept of private sector investment, public sector investment, two countries involved and thousands of good-paying jobs. Proud to say: launched it, powered up. Starting in June, I think we had the ribbon cutting.
 And so that's what you do when you don't let anything get in your way. All the obstacles that were not overcome before, you just power through it. And that's the ambition that I have with the people in this room who have the ability to make investments. And it'll be smart money to invest, for sure, in a place like New York, because I'll break down any barrier that stands in our way of doing what I need to do to support my economy, to keep the lights on, to drive down costs for consumers and create thousands of good-paying clean energy jobs. So we're ambitious. We're going to keep doing this.
 I’ve got all kinds of stuff here I could tell you, but I need you. We need the investors for the capital. Let's just be real candid here. A lot of money in this room. I can smell it. This is New York. I need your help. I need you to step up. I need you to be engaged with our administration. We'll tell you what our ambitions are, we'll tell you where we're heading, and we're heading where few are willing to go. We're going all the way. And I'm even going so far that I'm going to build more nuclear in the State of New York than the entire country has in 30 years. That's ambition, but it'll be executed upon.
 And in fact, I'm waiting for approvals from the Trump administration now to move ahead with the next step. My first conversation with the President, right after he got elected, said, "Let's do two things together. Penn Station looks like hell, scares everybody, let's make it nice." We're working on that. And I said, "I want to build nuclear." And he was a little surprised to hear that because Democrats don't usually talk about nuclear, because everybody still thinks it's Three Mile Island and China Syndrome and all these other scary specters. I saw the same movies. It was scary for a little while, except the technology has evolved dramatically, gotten smarter, more manageable and technologically safe. So I want to build up my grid because I've also got a lot of other challenges.
 We're going to move ahead with that, and I've got data centers that are coming. Now, I have proposals for even in one county, St. Lawrence County up on the St. Lawrence River, beautiful area, five data centers want to go there. We estimated that if all five of those data centers were approved, that would consume all the power that I would generate with one of my brand-new nuclear reactors. So there's no real economic benefit to the larger economy or to my local ratepayers or the other businesses like Micron, which is bringing 50,000 jobs to Upstate New York and even more we're announcing. So I will use energy to power smart economic projects, but data centers, we have a moratorium in place for one year, and after that year, we're going to have the smartest policy in the country. We're already starting to unveil it now.
 Because if you come — and it's up to local governments, it's up to them — but I'm going to help them negotiate. Because they go to a small town, and sometimes they got a part-time mayor and a part-time economic developer. They're supposed to negotiate a deal for their residents against these gigantic conglomerates? It doesn't work. So I'm saying, “No more tax breaks because I know you don't need them. You're going to bring your own power, or you're going to pay a significant amount into our overall grid to build resiliency in our transmission lines, help even subsidize the community and their ratepayers and their utility bills. You're going to have community benefits that you're going to give a million dollars per megawatt of power you're using — a lot of them over a hundred megawatts — hundred million dollars going to one of my local communities, upstate New York.” I'm not saying whether they should do it or not. It's a local decision. But I'm going to make sure that it's done in a smart way, uses less energy.
 And lastly, I'll close with this. I have sat with the leaders of these giant companies, almost every one of them. And I have challenged them. And I have said this: "You've created a technology that is capable of changing civilization as we know it. It's happening before our eyes: how we live, how we work, how we communicate. Ask AI how AI can be powered in a smarter way." Okay? Think about it. Does it have to be taking up seven miles of space, which is a proposal out in, I think, Arizona or Texas? Do you have to consume that much space? Do you need to use any water at all? Use the closed-loop systems, I know that's already in place. Do you have to make so much noise? Can you go vertical? Can you do something from satellites? Can you do it underwater? Just do something brilliant.
 I understand the need to power AI. I get it. But when you're looking to come and consume massive amounts of land and energy, the communities have to come out ahead of that. And you show me how. Show me how. My family — I have seven family members who live in Loudoun County, Virginia. You may have heard of it because it was the fastest-growing county because they're building houses on farmland, and they all moved there when they couldn't get jobs in Buffalo. Now they have gigantic data centers in their backyards. So I've seen this. This is not something that is hypothetical. It is real. So that's why I, as the Governor of the State of New York, know that there's smart ways to do things, and there are ways that let people go unregulated, do what they want, and they'll always find the cheapest way to get around with it. I get it. But you're not going to do something like this and not have my taxpayers and my residents come out ahead. So thank you, Mindy, for the opportunity just to talk about our ambition here in New York. Appreciate you very much.

title: Governor Kathy Hochul
text:
Media 

 August 28, 2026 

 Albany, NY

 Audio & Rush Transcript: Governor Hochul Discusses Tariffs, ICE and Social Media on MSNOW’s Morning Joe 

 Audio & Rush Transcript: Governor Hochul Discusses Tariffs, ICE and Social Media on MSNOW’s Morning Joe 

 Governor Hochul: “We passed a law and it went into effect just this week: You cannot have those agreements with ICE to be using local cops. [...] I want local cops focused on local crimes. And crime has gone down dramatically since I've been governor in the State of New York for the last five years, and it's because I've invested money in law enforcement. We're building trust between communities and law enforcement. [It] has nothing to do with having our local police diverted from catching the rapists, catching the murderers, responding to an emergency, and doing ICE's job for them. It's an $85 billion agency. I think they can take care of themselves.”
 Hochul: “It is absolutely appalling that when the war in Iran starts taking a bad turn, he decides to launch a war on our best friend in Canada, just to try and divert. And it is so unfair because the communities that I grew up in, from Buffalo and then all along Lake Ontario, which is still Lake Ontario, want to make that point, all the way up to Plattsburgh — our economies are so intertwined. And it's not a foreign country. Those are our neighbors. They come over to our sporting events, the Buffalo Bills games, the Sabres games. [...] Our costs for our local governments and our farmers and our businesses and people in the grocery stores are paying more now because of these tariffs.”

 Earlier today, Governor Hochul was a Guest on MSNOW's “Morning Joe.”
 AUDIO: The Governor's remarks are available in audio form here. 
 A rush transcript of the Governor's remarks is available below: 
 Willie Geist, MSNOW: Governor Hochul, great to see you this morning. Let's start right there with the decision, the settlement from Meta up to $17 billion. The hope was that this now would set the standard, YouTube, TikTok, Snap, others would fall in behind, and that social media would be made safer, especially for young people. What is your take on how significant this move is and what might come next?
 Governor Hochul: I would call it an important step in the right direction, Willie, but in New York State, we've actually gone further in many respects. I launched an initiative last year and the year before and the year before that, to try and rein in the excesses of social media when it came to really destroying many of our children's mental health. And first of all, I want to applaud all the families that stepped forward here with their stories of losing children to suicide and depression, and the young people came forward to help us get to this place. But I would say [it’s] an important step, but I think there's still going to be an important role for states and ultimately the federal government someday, when they feel like they have time to do something other than rename lakes. I would like to see a better focus at the government level to regulate this and bring in all the platforms.
 In New York State, all the platforms are covered by our first-in-the-nation rules saying no addictive algorithms can be bombarding our young people under the age of 18. You can have no notifications at all after midnight. Our kids need to get to sleep. And what helped all of this was our — separate from the social media company, we don't allow cell phones in schools. From the day that child walks — the second they walk in the door to the second they walk out — and that has done a lot to restore the mental health of our students in New York State. But I think it's a good settlement, but we're not done. We're not done. This fight is not over.
 Willie Geist, MSNOW: Yeah, this may be a good step, but as you point out, many people are skeptical about these companies policing themselves and creating rules that might cut into their profits, which ultimately, as we know from all the whistleblower documents, is really all they cared about, the child safety be damned. So what is the role, do you think, of the federal government? You're doing it on a state level, but what could the federal government be doing better to help keep kids safe on social media?
 Governor Hochul: Right. I'll give, I'll send the federal government — whoever wants to see it — the New York State laws, we've done this for years now. And focus on everything from banning access to AI chatbots — these young people are developing relationships, their first relationship is not with a human being anymore, and we have to save them from that — we also believe that no child should have their personal data monetized. These are bombarding our kids, capturing information about them so they can sell them products later. We don't allow that in the State of New York either. So I would very happily share the laws we've passed in New York, which is why we were named by Jonathan Haidt's organization, the number one state in America for protecting the mental health of young people. I'm proud of that, but we never rest on our laurels, and we're always trying to stay ahead of the next curve because they're out there trying to make money, and I'm trying to protect kids as New York's first mom governor.
 Willie Geist, MSNOW: And we'll see if these other companies fall in line, YouTube and the others. Let's turn to immigration, Governor. ICE arrests have surged to record levels this summer, reaching 43,000 in June, 49,000 in July. That's according to newly released federal data. An analysis from The New York Times shows most people arrested last month had no criminal charge or conviction, while fewer than 4% had a past violent conviction. 4%. Arrests have risen across the country with Texas averaging more than 380 per day and Florida more than 230. New Jersey, New Mexico also have seen arrests double. So Governor, this data from the federal government confirms what we already knew, which is that this administration is not going after the worst of the worst. We've seen just in the last week these scenes at bus stops around schools in Connecticut. We've seen scenes in hospital rooms where a mother and a daughter were arrested in hospital gowns after getting into a car accident. So what does the relationship in your state look like between law enforcement on the state level and ICE coming in from the federal level?
 Governor Hochul: Let me just step back for a second. You absolutely hit on this, Willie. Everybody who voted for Donald Trump believed he was going after the worst of the worst. That's what he promised. That was a flat-out lie. Because if he was going after the worst of the worst, I would think in the first few months they would've identified the known criminals, or those that they have charges against, or people who need to be extradited back to their country because of a criminal offense — now we're going after everybody from high school kids on Long Island to people going to their job on a farm, the home healthcare aides — we have devastated the home healthcare industry in the state of New York when we send back the Haitians who are very good at this work and they have relationships with senior citizens who are wondering why their aide did not show up the next day to take care of them.
 So what our relationship with law enforcement is — I will say this clearly because the Republicans are just absolutely lying about my position — New York State will never be a sanctuary for criminals. Full stop. We work with federal law enforcement, including ICE, when it comes to protecting New Yorkers, and that means we'll always have and always will work to get criminals off the streets and in the criminal justice system, get their justice, go to jail, and then go back to their home country. That's how we do it in New York.
 But what we had before was, there were counties that had relationships with ICE — formal agreements where they would actually be using local law enforcement for civil immigration enforcement. I'm not talking about criminals. I'm talking about someone who, the only offense is coming into this country, and these are people with temporary protective status. Maybe they had a green card, a work permit, married to an American citizen — they're going after everybody because they have to hit those inane Stephen Miller quotas.
 So I've said, and we passed a law and it went into effect just this week, you cannot have those agreements with ICE to be using local cops for doing your job, ICE. I want local cops focused on local crimes. And crime has gone down dramatically since I've been governor in the State of New York for the last five years, and it's because I've invested money in law enforcement. We're building trust between communities and law enforcement. It has nothing to do with having our local police diverted from catching the rapists, catching the murderers, responding to an emergency, and doing ICE's job for them. It's an $85 billion agency. I think they can take care of themselves.
 In fact, I wish they would just disband and go back to the old Immigration and Naturalization Service. Remember old INS? People trusted them. They did their jobs. This is a rogue policing state that is wreaking havoc across America. In New York, we say: No more.
 Mike Barnicle, MSNOW: So can you prevent the ICE, at the federal level, from securing agreements with local police forces in New York State?
 Governor Hochul: I just banned it. It's against the law now in the State of New York to have these agreements. The federal law that allows the creation of these agreements says “Subject to state and local laws.” State law just changed. So no more. No more. And we had to force every county that was participating — and I will say, the vast majority of counties in New York State were not. They were not participating, and those are among the safest counties in America. So the false argument that the Republicans continue to make — and DHS has been hitting me hard on this — they keep saying I've made New York State less safe. I'd rather stand with the criminals. That is full unadulterated BS.
 Mike Barnicle, MSNOW: Are they fighting this? Are the feds fighting this?
 Governor Hochul: No, they're just trying to fight me on social media. No, they can't stop us. I already did it. It's done.
 Ali Vitali, MSNOW: It's done.
 Governor Hochul: It's done.
 Ali Vitali, MSNOW: Something else that is happening, maybe not quite done, is this trade war that we see with Canada. I'm a New Yorker. I learned about trade, what we do on the world stage in elementary school. I know that about 13% of New York trade is done with Canada. I was struck by the fact that Senator Susan Collins in Maine said that she had received carve-outs or exemptions from the Canadians' retaliatory tariffs on seafood and fish products. And I wonder if New York State, if you are seeking any kinds of carve-outs to soften the blow on the New York economy.
 Governor Hochul: We're doing everything we can to soften the blow. And first of all, it is absolutely appalling that when the war in Iran starts taking a bad turn, he decides to launch a war on our best friend in Canada, just to try and divert. And it is so unfair because the communities that I grew up in, from Buffalo and then all along Lake Ontario, which is still Lake Ontario, want to make that point, all the way up to Plattsburgh — our economies are so intertwined. And it's not a foreign country. Those are our neighbors. They come over to our sporting events, the Buffalo Bills games, the Sabres games. Our farmers have great relationships. The manufacturing that goes on in the North Country, reliant on Canadian companies, Canadian steel, Canadian aluminum. And our wineries are suffering. I just sat down at the fair a couple days ago, talked to people who have the vineyards, they said the Canadians just stopped coming. So the tourism has dropped in all of our little towns in the North Country. They're not coming. Our relationship on the trade front is appalling now because our costs for our local governments and our farmers and our businesses and people in grocery stores are paying more now because of these tariffs.
 So it just has to stop. It just has to stop. So I will try to find at the sub-national level, relationships where I can find carve-outs. Absolutely doing that now. I've spoken to the other premiers. I've spoken to Mark Carney. When New Yorkers and Americans are experiencing some of the highest grocery prices, highest gasoline prices, highest utility rates — and we do get energy from Canada as well — to do something like this is just going to drive more people, I'm telling you right now, to the Democratic line. They are committing such an egregious political mistake as well, because people are going to rebel against this. I will be happy to remind them who is doing this, who drove up the costs in the grocery store when parents are trying to get the food for their kids' dinner tonight, or when they're trying to buy backpacks and the aluminum lunch pail is more expensive because the aluminum comes from Canada and they had a high tariff on it — this is what families are dealing with. This is what I'm trying to counter in New York with middle class tax breaks and a billion dollars in utility breaks for people coming in the mail shortly, inflation rebate checks. I'm trying to do what I can, put money back in people's pockets. At the same time, the Republicans are just sucking it right out, because they don't care. They don't care.
 Willie Geist, MSNOW: And Gene, of course, it's not like these tariffs are strategic in some way. There's no chessboard that we're looking at here. It's a temper tantrum from a man who's offended that Prime Minister Carney and others in Canada don't bend their knees, don't relinquish their national pride, that won't be a state. All of those things offend Donald Trump, so he slaps tariffs on a neighbor and an ally that raise prices in our country.
 Eugene Robinson, MSNOW: Yeah, it's not a chessboard. It's a checkerboard that the president just turned over because he wasn't winning. And it's insane. Governor Hochul, I'm old enough to remember when there was great pride in the fact that the US-Canada border was the longest unprotected border in the world. And people who live near the border on both sides have intertwined lives. There are people who live in the US and work in Canada, and vice versa, and the people are going back and forth across the bridge all the time. Has that changed? Is that being changed now because of this tension that has been created by President Trump and is a divorce underway?
 Governor Hochul: Oh, absolutely. And that's what's so sad about it, is for those of us who lived on the border and grew up with this expectation, you cross the Peace Bridge when you go to Chinese dinner in Fort Erie. You cross over to Canada. It's that close. You literally go into Canada for dinner sometimes. And they would come over and go to our fairs and our sporting events and our culturals. Three million fewer Canadians crossed the border into New York this past year. That's three million fewer people going up to the little shops in Lake Placid or Saranac Lake or coming to the Finger Lakes, to the wineries, as I mentioned. And even New York City — some of the hotels are telling me that the Canadians are just not coming, so they're not buying tickets on Broadway. So they are so offended, Gene, they are so insulted by how they've been treated by someone they considered their friend throughout our existence.
 And they don't understand — I think it's going to take a long time to heal this relationship. All of us in the states who border Canada — particularly New York here, we have a 430-mile border with Canada — we want to heal the relationship. We want to say, "That's not us." Except Donald Trump represents our government to them. And so only when he is gone can they understand that that's never who we were. We were never hostile to Canada. We appreciate the synergy that we have between New York State in particular and Canada, with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I'm doing what I can and we launched a campaign again in New York to try and entice visitors to come over and have discounts and flying flags and just saying, "Hey we love you." But I can understand. You try to make my state — if I was Canadian — make us the 51st state? That's pretty abusive. That's pretty abusive to someone who had been a longtime friend. So I'm just asking: Would you just stop? Divert your attention to something. Just stop, Mr. President. Just leave us alone. Try to start putting the genie back in the bottle so we can have the relationships that were once normal through my entire life. I don't know how long it's going to take, but we're not there yet. They're not coming over.
 Willie Geist, MSNOW: You're right. You're right, Governor. Americans love Canada. Just one man in Washington's having a tantrum at the moment. Democratic governor of New York, Kathy Hochul. Governor, thanks so much. We appreciate it.

español 

 State Fair 

 August 26, 2026 

 Albany, NY

 La Gobernadora Hochul Celebra la Inauguración de la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York 2026

 La Gobernadora Hochul Celebra la Inauguración de la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York 2026 

 Inaugura el Nuevo Edificio de la FFA de Nueva York para Conectar a los Visitantes con la Agricultura del Estado y Apoyar la Educación Agrícola Juvenil 

La Inversión Forma Parte del Compromiso de la Gobernadora de Impulsar el Crecimiento de la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York, Habiendo Destinado 119 Millones de Dólares Desde que Asumió el Cargo Hace Cinco Años 

Destaca Ofertas Agrícolas Nuevas y Recurrentes, Desde una Nueva Barra de Papas Hasta el Regreso de la Exhibición de Ganado Holstein 

La Feria Estatal Sigue Siendo un Espacio Asequible para que las Familias "se Desconecten de la Tecnología y Disfruten del Aire Libre" 

 La Gobernadora Kathy Hochul inauguró hoy la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York 2026, celebrando la apertura del nuevo edificio de la FFA y destacando una serie de ofertas y exhibiciones agrícolas, tanto nuevas como recurrentes, que acercarán aún más a los visitantes a la agricultura de Nueva York. La Gobernadora Hochul cortó la cinta inaugural del nuevo edificio de la FFA, de 10,500 pies cuadrados, el cual ayudará a formar a la próxima generación de líderes agrícolas y a apoyar la educación en este sector, una prioridad para la Gobernadora. El edificio de la FFA forma parte de una inversión de 34,7 millones de dólares en instalaciones agrícolas dentro del recinto ferial y de un compromiso total de 119 millones de dólares para mejoras generales del predio desde que ella asumió el cargo hace cinco años, en 2021. La Feria de este año se llevará a cabo desde el 26 de agosto hasta el lunes del Día del Trabajo (Labor Day), el 7 de septiembre de 2026, y sigue siendo la feria estatal más asequible del país, además de un espacio para que las familias "se desconecten de la tecnología y disfruten del aire libre".
 "Hay mucho que amar de la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York y, en esencia, es un lugar que realmente honra a la extraordinaria comunidad agrícola de Nueva York. Me enorgullecen las inversiones que hemos realizado en este espacio y en todo el recinto ferial durante los últimos cinco años", dijo la Gobernadora Hochul . “No se me ocurre una mejor manera de inaugurar la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York de 2026 que celebrando la apertura de un nuevo edificio de la FFA; esto permitirá que más jóvenes aprendan sobre esta importante industria y contribuyan a ella, al tiempo que ofrece a los asistentes la oportunidad de acercarse a la agricultura. Al abrir hoy las puertas, animo a los visitantes, tanto locales como de otros lugares, a explorar todo lo que la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York tiene para ofrecer”.
 Edificio de la FFA 
 El edificio de la FFA de Nueva York, situado en el extremo occidental del recinto ferial, es una instalación de 10,500 pies cuadrados que cuenta con un amplio espacio de exposición donde los estudiantes de la FFA pueden mostrar su trabajo a los asistentes a la feria, además de incluir áreas para conferencias y otras instalaciones. La construcción de este nuevo espacio se suma a los esfuerzos de la Gobernadora por apoyar a la Feria como un escaparate agrícola de primer nivel y fomentar la educación agrícola juvenil. La Gobernadora Hochul dio inicio oficialmente a las obras del edificio de la FFA la primavera pasada , como parte de la celebración del centenario de la FFA de Nueva York en su convención anual, celebrada en el propio recinto ferial.
 El nuevo edificio forma parte de un proyecto de 34,7 millones de dólares para mejorar las instalaciones agrícolas del recinto ferial de Syracuse, anunciado inicialmente por la Gobernadora en 2022. Además del edificio de la FFA, las mejoras incluyeron un nuevo espacio de exhibición para cabras —terminado hace dos años—, así como un nuevo establo para ovejas y centro de la lana y un nuevo establo para caballos, ambos finalizados el año pasado. El presupuesto del año fiscal 2026 destinó otros 35 millones de dólares a inversiones de capital en el recinto ferial; esto incluye la modernización de los escenarios de Chevy Court y Suburban Park para mejorar la experiencia de entretenimiento de los asistentes a conciertos, así como mejoras en el Expo Center para albergar festivales y eventos musicales durante todo el año. También se contempla un proyecto de renovación de 3,7 millones de dólares para el Milk Bar, situado en el edificio de productos lácteos (Dairy Products Building). Este nuevo proyecto, cuya finalización está prevista para la Feria de 2027, dotará al Milk Bar de una nueva imagen y ubicación, ampliando la superficie de exposición y permitiendo la instalación de equipos de última generación. En conjunto, esto permitirá que este elemento emblemático y tradicional de la Feria ofrezca leche de fresa, además de leche blanca y de chocolate, durante los 13 días que durarán las futuras ediciones del evento.
 El Comisionado de Agricultura del Estado de Nueva York, Richard A. Ball, dijo: "El nuevo edificio de la FFA ofrece a los visitantes la oportunidad de aprender sobre la agricultura y las numerosas oportunidades profesionales que brinda nuestra industria. Este espacio permitirá a los asistentes conectar con profesionales del sector, interactuar con sus compañeros de la FFA y ver de primera mano cómo los jóvenes pueden contribuir al futuro de la agricultura. Agradezco a la Gobernadora su compromiso con la Feria Estatal de Nueva York y su apoyo tanto a las exposiciones agrícolas como a todas las atracciones únicas, el entretenimiento emocionante y la deliciosa gastronomía que hacen que la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York sea verdaderamente excepcional".
 La directora de la Feria Estatal, Julie LaFave, dijo: "Desde nuestras tradiciones consagradas hasta nuestros nuevos eventos y atracciones, la Feria Estatal realmente ofrece algo para todos. Nuestro nuevo edificio de la FFA representa nuestro compromiso con la agricultura y es solo uno de los muchos espacios nuevos —distribuidos por diversas áreas del recinto ferial— que se podrán explorar este año. Nuestro equipo ha trabajado arduamente para ofrecer la feria más grande y mejor de todas, y nos entusiasma que los visitantes vengan a descubrir lo que tenemos preparado para 2026".
 La senadora estatal Michelle Hinchey dijo: "La Feria Estatal de Nueva York es una de las mejores celebraciones de la agricultura local; cada verano reúne a las familias para crear recuerdos inolvidables en el recinto ferial. Este año, es emocionante presenciar la gran inauguración del nuevo edificio de la FFA y ver las inversiones que estamos realizando en la próxima generación de la agricultura de Nueva York. Los visitantes también podrán disfrutar de comida deliciosa y atracciones divertidas, además de apoyar a pequeñas empresas de todo el estado. Agradezco a la gobernadora Hochul, al Departamento de Agricultura y Mercados, y a todos los vendedores que contribuyen a hacer de la Feria una tradición neoyorquina tan especial".
 La asambleísta Donna Lupardo dijo: "Cada año, la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York brinda la oportunidad de experimentar la agricultura, las tradiciones y la innovación que hacen que nuestro estado sea tan especial. El nuevo edificio de la FFA es una incorporación muy bienvenida a la Feria y ayudará a destacar a la próxima generación de líderes agrícolas, así como las numerosas oportunidades que ofrece esta industria. Espero con interés ver todas las nuevas exposiciones y mejoras, y animo a todos a asistir y disfrutar de la Feria".
 ¡Nuevas exposiciones y atracciones para 2026! 
 Además del nuevo edificio de la FFA, hay una gran variedad de exposiciones agrícolas y atracciones para visitar, incluidas muchas tradiciones clásicas, como la escultura de mantequilla, la leche perfectamente fría a 25 centavos en el *Milk Bar* y una gran cantidad de animales. Asimismo, para la Feria de 2026, los asistentes podrán disfrutar de varias novedades emocionantes . El concurso de ganado lechero Holstein —una de las actividades favoritas del público— se celebrará el domingo 30 de agosto en el Toyota Coliseum, contando con la mayor participación de ejemplares en casi una década. También en el Toyota Coliseum, los visitantes tendrán dos oportunidades para conocer más de cerca el maravilloso mundo de los caballos. El sábado 29 de agosto a las 10:30 a.m., los jóvenes de 4-H presentarán la Exhibición de Enganches y Caballos en Miniatura de 4-H, donde demostrarán sus habilidades de conducción de carruajes y manejo a pie. Luego, a las 5:00 p.m., los visitantes podrán unirse a los jóvenes de 4-H en un evento educativo para conocer a los magníficos caballos que se encuentran en la Feria.
 El viernes 28 de agosto, el sábado 29 de agosto y el sábado 5 de septiembre, los niños serán los protagonistas de la competencia de arrastre de tractores infantiles (*Kiddie Tractor Pull*) en el Toyota Coliseum. A partir del mediodía, esta versión a pequeña escala de la popular competencia de arrastre de tractores invita a los participantes inscritos a poner a prueba su fuerza y ver qué tan lejos pueden arrastrar sus tractores en este divertido evento.
 La Feria también estrena "Behind the Halter" (Detrás del Cabestro): una campaña digital que celebra a los jóvenes que representan a la próxima generación de la industria láctea de Nueva York. A través de pantallas ubicadas en el establo de ganado lechero, la campaña presentará a los asistentes a los jóvenes expositores que dedican innumerables horas al cuidado, preparación y exhibición de su ganado, ofreciendo una visión de la pasión y el arduo trabajo que hay detrás de los animales que se ven en la Feria.
 Y como una versión renovada de la tradición, los visitantes pueden acudir al puesto de papas de la Feria Estatal de Nueva York ( The Great New York State Fair Potato Booth ), recientemente rediseñado. Allí, el icónico puesto de papas a 1 dólar —ahora operado por Tully’s Good Times en colaboración con el programa "New York State Grown & Certified" del Departamento de Agricultura y Mercados del Estado de Nueva York— servirá las famosas papas al horno y las papas a la sal (ahora cultivadas en Nueva York), acompañadas de ingredientes provenientes de procesadores certificados por el programa estatal y utilizando leche de Nueva York. Esta colaboración coincide con la celebración del décimo aniversario del programa "NYS Grown & Certified".
 También hay una lista actualizada de vendedores y productores que ofrecen productos para degustación y venta en el mercado temporal (*pop-up*) y en el área comercial de Taste NY . Además, como novedad este año, el "New York State Tasting Yard" ofrecerá una selección ampliada de clases informativas en la sala de seminarios, impartidas por productores de bebidas artesanales de Nueva York.
 El jardín «Voice of the Farmer» (La voz del agricultor) también se ampliará para la Feria de 2026. Este año, el jardín incorporará nuevas parcelas de flores de corte —para destacar la creciente industria comercial de este sector en Nueva York—, una exhibición sobre el uso de gránulos de lana como enmienda para el suelo y un pequeño huerto de manzanos de alta densidad.
 La Feria sigue poniendo de relieve la agricultura mediante exposiciones y concursos agrícolas, con varias jornadas especiales dedicadas a destacar el sector, como el Día de las Carreras Agrícolas , el Día de la Carne de Vacuno , el Día del Arce , el Día de los Productos Lácteos y el regreso del Día de la Uva.
 La Feria Estatal de Nueva York de 2026 también presentará una variedad de nuevos espectáculos de entretenimiento en el recinto y artistas de primer nivel en sus escenarios. Desde un espectáculo de acrobacias que desafía la gravedad con motos de agua, esquí acuático y *wakeboard*, hasta adorables carreras de perros; pasando por el debut de "The Big Cheese", un mágico espectáculo de drones que ilumina el cielo; un nuevo Día STEAM y una programación ampliada para el Día del Orgullo LGBTQ+; hasta nuevas competiciones gastronómicas y entretenimiento lleno de acción en el Empire Room: la Feria de este año promete algo para todos los gustos. Consulte la lista completa de nuevas atracciones aquí .
 Todo esto se suma a las 41 actuaciones de artistas discográficos de renombre nacional que forman parte de la Chevrolet Music Series. Todos estos conciertos y espectáculos están incluidos en el precio de la entrada; con una única entrada de 8 dólares, los visitantes también tienen acceso a innumerables exposiciones agrícolas, una variada oferta gastronómica y mucho más.
 Acerca de la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York 
 La Feria comienza el miércoles 26 de agosto y se extiende hasta el Día del Trabajo (*Labor Day*), el lunes 7 de septiembre. Todos los conciertos están incluidos en el precio de la entrada. Las entradas ya están a la venta en el sitio web de la Feria: nysfair.ny.gov . Con una excelente relación calidad-precio, una entrada general cuesta 8 dólares e incluye acceso a todo el entretenimiento del recinto y a la galardonada programación de conciertos de la Feria. Además, existe una opción de entrada para visitantes frecuentes por 25 dólares.
 La Feria sigue siendo una de las más asequibles del país, manteniendo la entrada gratuita para personas mayores de 65 años y niños de 12 años o menos.
 Fundada en 1841, la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York exhibe lo mejor de la agricultura de Nueva York, ofrece entretenimiento de alta calidad y es una pieza clave de la estrategia estatal " CNY Rising ", destinada a impulsar la economía de la región central de Nueva York a través del turismo. Es la feria más antigua de Estados Unidos y figura constantemente entre las cinco mejores ferias estatales del país.
 El recinto ferial del estado de Nueva York (*New York State Fairgrounds*) es un complejo de exposiciones y entretenimiento de 375 acres que opera durante todo el año. Se invita al público a obtener más información sobre la Gran Feria Estatal de Nueva York en línea, ver fotos en Flickr y seguir la diversión en Facebook , TikTok , e Instagram .

title: Governor Kathy Hochul
text:
State Fair 

 August 26, 2026 

 Albany, NY

 Governor Hochul Celebrates the Opening of the 2026 Great New York State Fair

 Governor Hochul Celebrates the Opening of the 2026 Great New York State Fair 

 Cuts Ribbon on New York FFA Building To Help Connect Fairgoers to New York Agriculture, Support Youth Ag Education
 Investment is Part of The Governor’s Commitment to Growing the Great New York State Fair, Having Dedicated $119 Million Since Taking Office Five Years Ago
 Highlights New and Returning Agricultural Offerings, from New Potato Bar to Return of Holstein Show
 State Fair Continues To Be an Affordable Space for Families To ‘Get Offline, Get Outside’
 Traducción al español 

 Governor Kathy Hochul today kicked off The 2026 Great New York State Fair, celebrating the brand new FFA Building and highlighting a series of new and returning agricultural offerings and exhibits that will further connect fairgoers to New York agriculture. Governor Hochul cut the ribbon on the new 10,500 square-foot FFA Building, which will help develop the next generation of agricultural leaders and support agricultural education, a priority for the Governor. The FFA Building is part of a $34.7 million investment in agricultural facilities at the Fairgrounds and a commitment of $119 million for overall improvements to the grounds since she took office five years ago, in 2021. This year’s Fair will run from August 26 through Labor Day Monday, September 7, 2026, and continues to be the most affordable state fair in the nation, and a space for families to ‘Get Offline, Get Outside.’
 “There is so much to love about The Great New York State Fair, and at its core, it is a place that truly honors New York’s tremendous agricultural community. I’m proud of the investments we have made in this space and across the entire Fairgrounds over the last five years,” Governor Hochul said. “I can't think of a better way to kick off the 2026 Great New York State Fair than by celebrating the opening of a brand new FFA Building, which will allow more young people to learn about and contribute to this important industry while also providing fairgoers an opportunity to get closer to agriculture. As we open the gates today, I encourage visitors from near and far to explore all that the Great New York State Fair has to offer.”
 FFA Building 
 The New York FFA Building, located on the western end of the Fairgrounds, is a 10,500 square foot facility that features a large exhibition space for FFA students to showcase their work to fairgoers, and includes the addition of conference areas and more. The construction of this new space builds on the Governor’s efforts to support The Fair as a premier agricultural showcase and to support youth agricultural education. Governor Hochul officially broke ground on the FFA Building last spring as part of the New York FFA’s 100th anniversary celebration at its annual convention, which was held at the Fairgrounds.
 The new building is part of a $34.7 million project to improve agricultural facilities at the Fairgrounds in Syracuse, first announced by the Governor in 2022. In addition to the FFA Building, improvements also included a new show space for goats, completed two years ago, as well as a new Sheep Barn and Wool Center, new horse barn, both of which were completed last year. The Fiscal Year 2026 Budget provided an additional $35 million in capital investments at the Fairgrounds, including upgrading stages at Chevy Court and Suburban Park to enhance the Fair’s entertainment experiences for concertgoers and the Expo Center for year-round festivals and music events, as well as a $3.7 million renovation project of the Milk Bar in the Dairy Products Building. The new project, which is slated to be completed for the 2027 Fair, will include a new look and new location for the Milk Bar, increasing the square footage of the exhibit and allowing for the installation of new state-of-the-art equipment. Together, these will allow the longtime Fair staple to provide strawberry milk, along with white and chocolate milk, for all 13 days of future Fairs.

 https://www.youtube.com/embed/XkX1s46Xu20

 Audio 

 Photos 

 New York State Agriculture Commissioner Richard A. Ball said, “The new FFA Building offers fairgoers the chance to learn about agriculture and the many career opportunities our industry has to offer. The space will provide fairgoers with a chance to connect with industry professionals, engage with their peers in FFA, and see first-hand how young people can contribute to the future of agriculture. I thank the Governor for her commitment to the New York State Fair and for supporting its agricultural exhibits as well as all the Fair’s unique attractions, exciting entertainment, and delicious food that truly make the Great New York State Fair beyond great.”
 State Fair Director Julie LaFave said, “From our time-honored traditions to our new events and attractions, the State Fair truly offers something for everyone. Our new FFA Building represents our commitment to agriculture and is just one of the many new sites across many different areas to explore this year on the Fairgrounds. Our team has worked hard to provide the biggest and best State Fair this year and we’re excited for fairgoers to come see what we have in store for 2026.”
 State Senator Michelle Hinchey said, “The New York State Fair is one of the best celebrations of local agriculture, bringing families together every summer to make great memories on the fairgrounds. This year, it’s exciting to see the grand opening of FFA’s new building and the investments we’re making in next generation of New York agriculture. Visitors can also enjoy delicious food, fun attractions, and support small businesses from across New York. Thank you to Governor Hochul, Ag & Markets, and every vendor who helps make the Fair a special New York tradition.”
 Assemblymember Donna Lupardo said, “Each year, the Great New York State Fair provides an opportunity to experience the agriculture, traditions, and innovation that make our state so special. The new FFA Building is a welcome addition to the Fair and will help showcase the next generation of agricultural leaders and the many opportunities available in this industry. I’m looking forward to seeing all of the new exhibits and improvements, and encourage everyone to come out and enjoy the Fair.”
 2026 New Exhibits and Attractions! 
 In addition to the new FFA Building, there are plenty of agricultural exhibits and attractions to see, including scores of traditions, like the Butter Sculpture, perfectly chilled, $0.25 milk at the Milk Bar, and plenty of animals. Plus, for the 2026 Fair, fairgoers can experience several new and exciting additions . The Holstein Dairy Cattle Competition, a fairgoer favorite, will take place on Sunday, August 30 in the Toyota Coliseum with its largest showing in nearly a decade. Also in the Toyota Coliseum, fairgoers will get two opportunities to take a closer look at the wonderful world of horses. On Saturday, August 29 at 10:30 a.m., 4-H youth will present the 4-H Driving and Miniature Horse Show, where they will demonstrate their driving and in-hand skills. Then, at 5:00 p.m., visitors can join 4-H youth for a Meet the Horses Educational Event to learn more about the magnificent horses staying at The Fair.
 On Friday, August 28, Saturday, August 29, and Saturday, September 5, kids will take center stage for the Kiddie Tractor Pull in the Toyota Coliseum. Beginning at noon, this pint-sized version of the beloved tractor pull invites youth registrants to test their strength and see how far they can pull their tractors in this entertaining competition.

 “I can't think of a better way to kick off the 2026 Great New York State Fair than by celebrating the opening of a brand new FFA Building, which will allow more young people to learn about and contribute to this important industry while also providing fairgoers an opportunity to get closer to agriculture."

 Governor Kathy Hochul 

 The Fair is also debuting Behind the Halter — Celebrating the Youth Behind New York’s Dairy Cattle, a new digital campaign highlighting the young people who represent the next generation of New York’s dairy industry. Featured on screens throughout the Dairy Cattle Barn, the campaign will introduce Fairgoers to young exhibitors who dedicate countless hours to caring for, preparing and showing their dairy cattle, offering a glimpse into the passion and hard work behind the animals they see at The Fair.
 And for a new updated twist on tradition, fairgoers can visit the newly reimagined The Great New York State Fair Potato Booth , where The Fair’s iconic $1 potato, now operated by Tully’s Good Times in collaboration with the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets’ New York State Grown & Certified program, will be serving up The Fair’s famous baked potatoes, and salt potatoes, now grown in New York, with toppings sourced from New York State Grown & Certified processors, using New York milk. The collaboration comes as the NYS Grown & Certified Program celebrates its 10th anniversary.
 There is also a new updated list of vendors and producers offering product for sampling and sale at the Taste NY Pop-Up Market and Marketplace . Additionally, new this year: the New York State Tasting Yard will offer an expanded selection of informational classes in the Seminar Room, hosted by New York craft beverage producers.
 The Voice of the Farmer Garden is additionally expanding for the 2026 Fair. This year, the garden will newly include new cut flower beds highlighting New York’s growing commercial cut flower industry, an exhibit on wool pellets as soil amendments, and a small, high-density apple orchard.
 The Fair continues to highlight agriculture through agricultural exhibits and competitions, with several special days dedicated to highlighting the industry, including Agricultural Career Day , Beef Day , Maple Day , and Dairy Day , and the return of Grape Day.

 Embedded Flickr Album

 The 2026 New York State Fair will also be showcasing a variety of new grounds entertainment acts and top-notch performing artists on its entertainment stages. From a gravity-defying jet ski, waterski, and wakeboard gymnastics stunt show to adorable racing dogs, the debut of The Big Cheese, a magical drone show that lights up the sky, to a new STEAM Day and expanded LGBTQ+ Pride Day programming, to new food competitions and action-packed entertainment in the Empire Room, this year’s Fair promises something for everyone. See the complete list of new attractions. 
 This is all in addition to the 41 national recording acts that are a part of the Chevrolet Music Series. These concerts and entertainment acts are all included in the price of admission, with a single $8 admission ticket also giving fairgoers access to countless agricultural exhibits, diverse food choices, and so much more.
 About The Great New York State Fair 
 The Fair starts Wednesday, August 26, and runs through Labor Day, Monday, September 7. All concerts are included in the price of admission. Tickets are on sale now at The Fair’s website, nysfair.ny.gov . Packed with value, a single admission ticket costs $8 and includes access to all grounds entertainment and The Fair’s award-winning concert lineup. In addition, a Frequent Fairgoer ticket option is available for $25.
 The Fair continues to be one of the most affordable fairs in the nation, with admission remaining free for those aged 65 and older along with children 12 years old and under.
 Founded in 1841, The Great New York State Fair showcases the best of New York agriculture, provides top-quality entertainment, and is a key piece of the state’s CNY Rising strategy of growing the Central New York economy through tourism. It is the oldest fair in the United States and is consistently recognized as being among the top five state fairs in the nation.
 The New York State Fairgrounds is a 375-acre exhibit and entertainment complex that operates all year. Audiences are encouraged to learn more about The Great New York State Fair online, browse photos on Flickr , and follow the fun on Facebook , TikTok , and Instagram .

title: Governor Kathy Hochul

Economic Development 

 July 23, 2026 

 Albany, NY

 Governor Hochul Announces Applications Are Now Being Accepted for the $225 Million Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative

 Governor Hochul Announces Applications Are Now Being Accepted for the $225 Million Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative 

 Selected Projects Must Significantly Bolster Economic Development Throughout the City of Rochester and Monroe County
 Projects to be Funded Through the Governor’s FY 2027 Enacted Budget

 Governor Kathy Hochul today announced that applications are now being accepted for the $225 million Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative (RMTI). In the FY 2027 Enacted Budget, the Governor committed funding for the initiative, which will be administered by Empire State Development and support investments in transformative projects throughout Monroe County and the City of Rochester. This initiative will focus on projects that support economic development in the areas of strategic placemaking, adaptive reuse, innovation infrastructure, and public safety. Applications will be accepted through the Consolidated Funding Application Process and awarded on a rolling basis.
 “My administration is committed to driving economic growth that lifts up every corner of New York State,” Governor Hochul said. “We have already invested more than $500 million in projects throughout Monroe County, and this new initiative will build on that progress, keep the momentum going in Rochester and strengthen communities across Upstate.”
 In order to be considered for investment, potential projects must among other requirements: 
 have a transformational impact that will result in clear economic benefits such as job creation, increased visitation, expanded housing or commercial activity, improved public spaces, and/or strengthened neighborhood vitality;
 be highly visible and accessible, creating places or experiences that residents and visitors can readily engage with;
 create benefits that extend beyond the project site, contributing to Rochester and/or Monroe County’s broader revitalization and strengthening its role as a regional hub;
 leverage additional investment, having a clear path to leveraging private, philanthropic, or other public funding, maximizing the impact of state resources;
 demonstrate long-term operational and financial viability to ensure that state-funded investments remain assets well beyond initial implementation.
 A full list of RMTI requirements is available here. Additional questions may be directed to [email protected] .
 Within this year’s state budget, Governor Hochul also committed another $75 million to further support the buildout of High Falls State Park in downtown Rochester. In May 2026, the governor outlined the latest designs and framework that will bring the park to life. The 40-acre park, featuring the spectacular 80-foot waterfall, would be open year-round and include several distinct focal points to experience nature, gather with friends and family, and learn about Rochester’s heritage. Phased construction of the new park is expected to begin in late 2026.
 The total $300 million commitment in new funding for greater Rochester marks yet another example of the Governor’s focus on the Finger Lakes region. Since 2021, she has committed more than half a billion dollars in investments that are supporting economic development in the region including ROC The Riverway - a partnership between New York State and the City of Rochester to revitalize the Genesee River downtown waterfront. Phase two of ROC The Riverway was launched by Governor Hochul in 2022 and highlighted by the establishment of the new state park which had been off limits to the public for generations due to its formal industrial uses. To date, NYS has invested more than $100 million towards dozens of riverway projects, several of which have been completed, including the Brewery Line Trail extension and Pont de Rennes Bridge renovation within the High Falls area.
 Other Transformational Regional Investments Include: 
 Since 2021, under Governor Hochul’s leadership, New York State has committed nearly $560 million in major capital projects within Monroe County, including:
 $100 million commitment for Inner Loop North project that will connect neighborhoods, fostering development, and creating green space further revitalizing the city's core.
 $59.6 million for upgrades to the Joseph A. Floreano Rochester Riverside Convention Center that will include a new building along Main Street to provide a glass-fronted event space, LED display panel and much more.
 $50 million for the Strong Hospital Emergency Tower at University of Rochester Medical Center’s Strong Memorial Hospital.
 $50 million committed through Regional Revitalization Partnership that is investing in distressed neighborhoods, supporting small businesses, placemaking, and spurring workforce development.
 $42.5 million in investments to Seneca Park Zoo allowing for the modernization of the zoo, creating a world-class experience boosting local tourism.
 $40 million for electrical and wastewater infrastructure upgrades needed to support fairlife’s construction of a $650 million facility in the Town of Webster-another $21 million was made available through the Excelsior Jobs Tax Credit Program in exchange for a commitment to create approximately 250 new jobs.
 $18 million in phase two upgrades to the Frederick Douglass Greater Rochester International Airport that provided comprehensive upgrades to modernize the airport campus while expanding cultural and community spaces
 Monroe County Executive Adam Bello and City of Rochester Mayor Malik D. Evans said, “We’re grateful for Governor Kathy Hochul’s leadership and continued commitment to Monroe County and the City of Rochester. These investments will fuel economic development in our community and help drive job creation, support and attract local businesses, cultivate innovative economic development projects, and strengthen key industries throughout Rochester and Monroe County. At a time when many communities are facing uncertainty, Governor Hochul continues to demonstrate confidence in our potential and belief in our local workforce. She is a true champion for Upstate communities, and we appreciate her partnership and leadership in prioritizing our economic growth. We look forward to working with our state delegation and local partners to ensure these resources deliver meaningful, lasting benefits for our residents, families, and business community.”
 FLREDC Co-Chairs, Greater Rochester Chamber of Commerce President Bob Duffy and Monroe Community College President DeAnna R. Burt-Nanna said, “This visionary new initiative complements the investment strategy cultivated over the last several years through the Finger Lakes Regional Economic Development Council process and supplements the dozens of economic development programs offered through the annual REDC process. As always, we remain grateful to Governor Hochul for her unwavering commitment as we work towards an incredibly exciting future for everyone that calls this community home.”
 Overall, Governor Hochul’s FY 2027 Enacted Budget once again included record investments to support New Yorkers — without raising income taxes; builds on the success of her Affordability Agenda, invests in the next generation with the highest level school-aid support in state history; commits to protecting access to health and mental health care without shifting costs to families and without jeopardizing access to care for New York’s most vulnerable; further builds on her efforts to support affordable housing projects; includes investments to bolster public safety; supports economic development investments in key industries to support New York’s workers, bolster businesses and build on this economic growth; and will work to ensure that no New Yorker goes hungry among other initiatives.
 Empire State Development President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said, “Governor Hochul has been a constant champion for Upstate New York. The Rochester-Monroe County Transformation Initiative will work to establish a solid foundation upon which the city and county can build an exciting future. Through our valued partnerships with local stakeholders, and through the regional council process, we are supporting transformational projects that represent the needs of all who live in the region, encouraging even more people to experience all that it has to offer.”
 State Senator Jeremy Cooney said, “The Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative (RMTI) is a monumental win for Upstate New York’s economic development. Supporting these projects means building our workforce, improving public spaces, and expanding opportunities for New Yorkers – an impact that will be felt across the entire region. This initiative is a testament to Governor Hochul’s commitment to investing in Upstate communities, and I’m grateful for her continued support.”
 State Senator Samra Brouk said, “The Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative is a critical $225 million investment in impactful projects throughout the city and Monroe County. I applaud Governor Hochul for building upon her commitment to uplifting Upstate New York by prioritizing job opportunities, housing and commercial needs, and neighborhood improvements to help our residents thrive.”
 Assemblymember Harry Bronson said, “The Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative demonstrates a commitment to community-driven economic development, job creation, housing and initiatives that will benefit economic sectors and families throughout the area. I am proud of the work we’ve done as a State Delegation, with the support and partnership of Governor Hochul, Monroe County Executive Bello and Rochester Mayor Evans to foster robust regional economic growth through bold new opportunities that will revitalize and secure our communities and strengthen our region for generations.”
 Assemblymember Demond Meeks said, “Investing in our city’s infrastructure, public safety, and green spaces is vital to the long-term vitality of Rochester and Monroe County. With applications now open for the $225 million Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative, our local organizations, entrepreneurs, and community leaders have a direct opportunity to drive transformative change. I thank Governor Hochul for prioritizing the Finger Lakes region in this year’s state budget, and I strongly encourage eligible partners across our community to submit their projects through the Consolidated Funding Application process.”
 Assemblymember Sarah Clark said, “The Rochester-Monroe Transformation Initiative gives our community a rare opportunity to make investments that will shape the next generation of growth across Rochester and Monroe County. The projects supported through this funding will strengthen neighborhoods, create jobs, attract additional private investment, and create lasting results for our region.  Assemblymember Jen Lunsford said, “State investment in economic development is critical to ensuring that our region can keep pace with growth by expanding job opportunities, tourism, and creating the infrastructure our residents and businesses need to thrive.  Governor Hochul, Amtrak and New York State Department of Transportation Announce Tickets Now on Sale for Direct Train Service to Great New York State Fair

 Governor Hochul, Amtrak and New York State Department of Transportation Announce Tickets Now on Sale for Direct Train Service to Great New York State Fair 

 Daily Train Service Offers Convenient and Cost-Effective Way for Fairgoers To Travel to Upstate New York’s Largest Agricultural and Entertainment Event

 Governor Kathy Hochul, in collaboration with Amtrak and the New York State Department of Transportation, today announced that tickets are now on sale for direct train service to and from The Great New York State Fair. Daily train service allows State Fair visitors a safe, convenient and environmentally friendly travel option to experience one of New York’s signature summer events. The Great New York State Fair features agricultural exhibits, musical performances from top artists, mouth-watering food and fun for the whole family as the most affordable state fair in the country. Throughout The Fair’s 13-day duration, Amtrak trains will make five daily stops starting Wednesday, August 26 and continuing through Labor Day, Monday, September 7. Tickets are available now at Amtrak.com , via the Amtrak mobile app, at the station ticket counters, or by calling 1-800-USA-RAIL.
 “Nothing says summer in New York like the Great New York State Fair, with its spectacular exhibits, musical performances, delicious food and exciting rides and games,” Governor Hochul said. “It’s something everyone should experience firsthand and taking the train makes that even easier. Riding the rails gets you right to The Fair’s doorstep without the hassles of driving. It’s easy, convenient and affordable. So get on board and come to The Great New York State Fair. You won’t regret it.”
 By taking the train, visitors will save on gas, traffic and parking fees by arriving steps from The Fairgrounds via select Empire Service and Maple Leaf trains, which will make daily stops at The State Fair (in between stops at Rochester and Syracuse stations). To purchase tickets, customers should select the “NYF” destination on Amtrak’s website; tickets are only available on dates when the fair is open. Train service to The Fair includes:
 Maple Leaf Train 63 – Departs Moynihan Train Hall at 7:15 a.m. and arrives at The Fair at 1:11 p.m.
 Maple Leaf Train 64 – Departs Toronto at 8:20 a.m. and arrives at the Fair at 2:29 p.m.
 Empire Service Train 281 – Departs Moynihan Train Hall at 10:20 a.m. and arrives at The Fair at 4:21 p.m.
 Empire Service Train 283 – Departs Moynihan Train Hall at 1:20 p.m. and arrives at The Fair at 7:13 p.m.
 Empire Service Train 284 – Departs Niagara Falls at 6:27 a.m. and arrives at The Fair at 9:29 a.m.
 New York State Department of Transportation Commissioner Marie Therese Dominguez said, “The Great New York State Fair is always a highlight of the summer and NYSDOT is proud to once again partner with Amtrak to bring fairgoers to this exciting, family friendly event. Traveling to The Fair by train is affordable, fun and good for the environment. It’s also easy, as Amtrak drops you right off at The Fair’s doorstep! Whether you’re traveling from Buffalo, New York City, or points in between, leave the driving to Amtrak and come enjoy all that The Great New York State Fair has to offer. See you at The Fair.”
 New York State Agriculture Commissioner Richard A. Ball said, “The Great New York State Fair is where communities come together. Every year, The Fair gives visitors a chance to connect with the people and products that make our state so special. We’re grateful for our continued partnership with Amtrak and NYSDOT, and look forward to welcoming fairgoers for a 13-day celebration of agriculture, entertainment and family fun.”
 New York State Fair Director Julie LaFave said, “We want The Great New York State Fair to be part of everyone’s summer plans. By partnering with Amtrak and NYSDOT, The Fair as a destination is more accessible than ever, with the comfort and convenience travelers have come to know. We’re excited to invite families, friends and visitors from across New York and beyond to experience all the fun, food and festivities that make The Fair a beloved summer tradition.”
 Amtrak Executive Vice President, Strategy & Planning Jennifer Mitchell said, “The annual tradition of Amtrak, NYSDOT, and the Governor partnering to deliver convenient, comfortable travel to The Great New York State Fair proudly continues for another summer. Whether you need to relax before or after fun games, thrilling rides and great food, Amtrak has the large, spacious seats, picturesque windows and direct service to The Fair where you can unwind without having to sit in traffic.
 Direct train service to The Great New York State Fair has been offered by Amtrak since 2002. Customers can save when booking online at least five days in advance of travel with Amtrak’s See NY and Save discount, in addition to everyday discounts for kids, seniors, military members and more. Passengers can enjoy free Wi-Fi with excellent service, spacious Business Class seats, a café car and ample leg room.
 The Great New York State Fair opens Wednesday, August 26 and continues through Labor Day, September 7. Admission is $8 plus fees for adults. Tickets are free for adults ages 65 and over and children ages 12 and under. Tickets include access to all grounds entertainment, agricultural competitions and exhibits and admission to concerts in Chevy Court and Suburban Park.
 Founded in 1841, The Great New York State Fair showcases the best of New York agriculture, provides top-quality entertainment, and is a key piece of the State’s CNY Rising strategy of growing the Central New York economy through tourism. It is the oldest fair in the United States and is consistently recognized as being among the top five state fairs in the nation.
 The New York State Fairgrounds is a 375-acre exhibit and entertainment complex that operates all year. Audiences are encouraged to learn more about The Great New York State Fair online, browse photos on Flickr , and follow the fun on Facebook , TikTok , and Instagram.
